events.title: The Fourth Council of Constantinople opens
events.shortBlurb: Legates of Pope Hadrian II opened in Hagia Sophia the council the West would number as the eighth general synod, called to end the affair of Photius…
body: The patriarch Ignatius, deposed and exiled years before, had been restored by the new emperor Basil the Macedonian; the intruded Photius, who had gone so far as to pronounce the deposition of Pope Nicholas I in 867, was confined to a monastery. Both emperor and patriarch asked Rome for a general council, and Hadrian II sent three legates to preside in his name.

On 5 October 869 the council opened in the cathedral of Holy Wisdom, the pope's legates in the first seats. The fathers were never many — little more than a hundred bishops in all — and over ten sessions, the last on 28 February 870, they reconciled the penitent, heard a silent and unyielding Photius, renewed his condemnation, and subscribed the old formula of Hormisdas binding its signers to the Apostolic See.

Western canonists number this as the eighth ecumenical council, though the East has not received it into her synodal books. Within a decade Ignatius was dead and Photius reigned again in his place, and a further council in 879 undid much of what the council of 869 had decreed.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Constantinople, Fourth Ecumenical Council of”
